query: For multicomponent high-entropy alloys in solid and liquid states at and near their high melting temperatures, what single testable methodological intervention could overcome the inability of EAM references to represent the many atomic configurations of the ab initio liquid? Explain why it should improve reference–target phase-space overlap, predict the reduction in thermodynamic-integration path mismatch relative to TOR-TILD’s EAM references, define the applicable composition and temperature ranges, identify supporting evidence from elemental or binary calculations, and specify a decisive free-energy benchmark that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Replacing the traditional EAM reference in the TOR-TILD thermodynamic integration framework with a deep neural network potential (DNNP) trained on diverse ab initio liquid configurations will improve the reference–target phase-space overlap and reduce the integration path mismatch for multicomponent high-entropy alloys near their melting temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic or near-equiatomic high-entropy alloys (e.g., refractory HEAs) in both solid and liquid states at temperatures close to their high melting points (approximately 0.9Tm to Tm).
generation.intervention: Substitute the EAM reference potential with a deep neural network potential specifically trained on an extensive set of ab initio liquid configurations to capture many-body and anharmonic effects.
generation.conditions: Applicable to multicomponent (five or more elements) high-entropy alloys where the melting temperature is high (e.g., refractory compositions), and the operating temperature range is near the melting point (roughly from 0.9Tm to Tm).
generation.structural_mediator: The deep neural network potential acts as a structural mediator by encapsulating the complex atomic interactions and configurational diversity of the liquid state.
generation.mechanism: By training on a comprehensive ab initio dataset that includes the many different atomic configurations of the liquid, the DNNP better represents many-body interactions and anharmonic contributions. This enhanced representation improves the phase-space overlap between the reference and target systems, thereby reducing the mismatch in the thermodynamic integration path compared to conventional EAM references.
generation.predicted_outcome: A reduction in the thermodynamic integration path mismatch by an estimated 30–50% compared to the TOR-TILD method using EAM references, leading to more accurate free energy determinations.
generation.baseline: The existing TOR-TILD methodology that employs EAM potentials, which have limited capability in representing the full ab initio configurational space of the liquid.
generation.boundary: This approach is expected to be most effective for compositions that are typical of high-melting, entropy-stabilized systems. Its performance may be limited in alloys that exhibit extreme short-range ordering or where the training data for the DNNP is insufficiently representative.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of the reduction in integration path mismatch is uncertain and may vary with the specific alloy system and quality of the ab initio training dataset used for the DNNP.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct parallel thermodynamic integration studies on a selected high-entropy alloy near its melting temperature. One set of integrations will use the conventional EAM reference within the TOR-TILD framework, while the other set will use the DNNP reference trained on extensive ab initio liquid configurations. Compare the free energy calculations and convergence metrics between the two approaches.
measurements: Total free energy computed via thermodynamic integration
Metrics of phase-space overlap (e.g., statistical distributions of sampled configurations)
Convergence rate of the integration path
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the DNNP approach does not achieve at least a 30% reduction in the integration path mismatch or does not show a statistically significant improvement in phase-space overlap and convergence rates compared to the EAM-based method, then the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractThe efficient energy use in multiple sectors of modern industry is partly based on the efficient use of high-strength, high-performance alloys that retain remarkable mechanical properties at elevated and high temperatures. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) represent the most recent class of these materials with a high potential for high-temperature high-strength applications. Aside from their chemical composition and microstructure-property relationship, limited information on the effect of heat treatment as a decisive factor for alloy design is available in the literature. This work intends to contribute to this research topic by investigating the effect of heat treatment on the microstructure and mechanical performance of an Al4.4Co26Cr19Fe18Ni27Ti5.6 HEA. The solution annealed state is compared to aged states obtained at different heat treatment times at 750 °C. The temporal evolution of the matrix and the γ’-precipitates are analyzed in terms of chemical composition, crystallography, size, shape, and volume fraction by means of scanning electron microscopy, transmission electron microscopy, and atom probe tomography. The melting temperature is a crucial property of materials that determines their potential applications in different industrial fields. In this study, we used a deep neural network potential to describe the structure of high-entropy (TiZrTaHfNb)CxN1−x carbonitrides (HECN) in both solid and liquid states. This approach allows us to predict heating and cooling temperatures depending on the nitrogen content to determine the melting temperature and analyze structure changes from atomistic point of view. A steady increase in nitrogen content leads to increasing melting temperature, with a maximum approaching for 25% of nitrogen in the HECN. A careful analysis of pair correlations, together with calculations of entropy in the considered liquid phases of HECNs allows us to explain the origin of the nonlinear enhancement of the melting temperature with increasing nitrogen content. The maximum melting temperature of 3580 ± 30 K belongs to (TiZrTaHfNb)C0.75N0.25 composition. The improved melting behavior of high-entropy compounds by the addition of nitrogen provides a promising way towards modification of thermal properties of functional and constructional materials.

Recently, a new alloy design concept based on entropic contributions to the thermodynamic landscape, rather than cohesive energy, was proposed, which was subsequently extended to non-metallic systems such as multicomponent oxides. This strategy was explored by deliberately incorporating five or more elemental species into a single lattice with random site occupancy. Due to the engineered configuration disorder, these entropy-stabilized solid solution alloys, that is, high-entropy alloys (HEAs), usually show a single-phase structure with high symmetry and extremely attractive properties. Among various reported HEAs in literature, the equiatomic CoCrFeMnNi alloy (also termed as Cantor's alloy) is a prototype fcc (face-centred-cubic) HEA, which possesses ultrahigh fracture toughness and large ductility, even at cryogenic temperatures. It is generally believed that HEA lattices are severely distorted and atomic diffusion is extremely sluggish due to the chemical complexity and packing disorder. It is important to consider that the metal carbide precursors have very strong covalent/ionic bonds, and are therefore enthalpy stabilized. However, the same might not be the case for their mixture. In fact, a statistical analysis of the AFLOW.org enthalpies indicates that the gain in formation enthalpy by adding mixing species, ΔHf(N + 1) − ΔHf(N), decreases with N, and can easily be overcome by the monotonic increase in entropy-gain for the disordered systems (to go from order to complete or partial disorder). In the AFLOW analysis, the threshold between low- and high-entropy systems is around four mixing species. To have completely entropy-stabilized materials, five mixing species are required (similar to the Entropy-Stabilized Oxides). For carbides in which only the metal-sublattice is randomly populated, five metals should be enough to achieve carbide entropy stabilization, especially at equi-composition. Notably, if other sublattices were also allowed to contain disorder, (e.g., reciprocal systems like TaxHf1−xC1−y,), then the overall number of species might reduce.
